steps.instruction: Drain the chilled sheets well, and coat each side lightly with vegetable oil so they do not stick together. They can be held up to 3 hours; for holding, spread them on a parchment-lined baking tray and separate sheet layers with plastic wrap.

As an alternative only for no-boil sheets, soak them in warm water for 30 minutes to partially hydrate, then drain using paper towels or kitchen towels. This alternative does not also require boiling and ice-bathing the same sheets.

With the 1.5 L warm ragù already prepared, heat the oven to 375°F (190°C). Butter a 9-by-13-inch baking dish. Cover its base with a thin even coating of ragù, then lay on pasta sheets. Small overlaps are fine; cut oversized sheets to avoid unnecessary double-thickness areas.

Spread another very thin coating of ragù over the sheets, leaving the pasta visible through the sauce in a few places. Drizzle on a little béchamel, then scatter grated Parmigiano-Reggiano. Continue alternating pasta, ragù, béchamel and grated cheese until the dish is filled, approximately 6 layers. Finish with a pasta layer covered evenly with all remaining béchamel, and grate a generous final covering of cheese over it.

Bake about 35 minutes, stopping when the sauce bubbles and the top is browned. A rimmed baking tray beneath the dish can catch overflow. Rest the lasagna for 10 minutes after baking before cutting and serving.

Lasagna Bolognese | Daniel Gritzer | Serious Eats
Source timing:prep15min cook65min total80min; yield8servings,9-by-13-inch dish.
INGREDIENTS
4 tablespoons unsalted butter (2 ounces; 60 g), plus more for greasing baking dish
4 tablespoons all-purpose flour (1.25 ounces; 35 g)
3 cups (700 ml) whole milk
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
Pinch freshly grated nutmeg
2 pounds (900 g) fresh homemade plain egg or spinach pasta or store-bought fresh lasagna noodles, or 2 (450 g) boxes dry lasagna noodles (see note)
Vegetable oil, for greasing pasta
1 1/2 quarts (1.5 L) warm ragù bolognese
3 ounces (85 g) Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese
In a pot of salted boiling water (instructions)
transfer immediately to a large ice bath (instructions)
If Using No-Boil Pasta: Soak in warm water for 30 minutes (instructions)
METHOD (all operational details reexpressed, not untouched HTML)
1. Use a small saucepan on medium-high heat to melt the butter, stopping it from browning. Whisk in flour to make a paste, and stir about 1 minute until the uncooked flour smell disappears. Add milk while whisking continuously, either pouring a thin steady stream or adding a few tablespoons per addition. Whisk into the corners as well, keeping the mixture uniform. It first thickens substantially, then becomes thin when the milk has all been incorporated.
2. Continue stirring while heating until the sauce starts simmering and thickens a little. Turn heat down to low, and cook with stirring for about 3 minutes, stopping when a thin coating stays on the back of a wooden spoon.
3. Add salt and black pepper, then whisk in nutmeg. Whisk away any small lumps; stubborn larger lumps can be removed with an immersion or countertop blender. Either use the white sauce immediately or cover its surface directly with plastic wrap and hold it warm. Alternatively refrigerate in a sealed container for several days and reheat very gently on the stovetop or in the microwave.
4. For homemade fresh pasta only, use the linked Serious Eats fresh-pasta dough recipe through its step 10, making twice that recipe to obtain 2 pounds of sheets. Cut long sheets into rectangles around 8 inches long. Having extra sheets avoids running short during assembly. Store-bought fresh or dry lasagna sheets are already allowed in the ingredient list and do not require making fresh dough.
5. For fresh or ordinary dry sheets, prepare a pot of salted boiling water. Cook in batches if needed until al dente; commercial sheets usually require about 1 minute less than their package direction. Lift them out with a spider or mesh strainer and immediately move them into a large ice-water bath.
6. Drain the chilled sheets well, and coat each side lightly with vegetable oil so they do not stick together. They can be held up to 3 hours; for holding, spread them on a parchment-lined baking tray and separate sheet layers with plastic wrap.
7. As an alternative only for no-boil sheets, soak them in warm water for 30 minutes to partially hydrate, then drain using paper towels or kitchen towels. This alternative does not also require boiling and ice-bathing the same sheets.
8. With the 1.5 L warm ragù already prepared, heat the oven to 375°F (190°C). Butter a 9-by-13-inch baking dish. Cover its base with a thin even coating of ragù, then lay on pasta sheets. Small overlaps are fine; cut oversized sheets to avoid unnecessary double-thickness areas.
9. Spread another very thin coating of ragù over the sheets, leaving the pasta visible through the sauce in a few places. Drizzle on a little béchamel, then scatter grated Parmigiano-Reggiano. Continue alternating pasta, ragù, béchamel and grated cheese until the dish is filled, approximately 6 layers. Finish with a pasta layer covered evenly with all remaining béchamel, and grate a generous final covering of cheese over it.
10. Bake about 35 minutes, stopping when the sauce bubbles and the top is browned. A rimmed baking tray beneath the dish can catch overflow. Rest the lasagna for 10 minutes after baking before cutting and serving.

notes: Prepared meat sauce is explicitly represented by a distinct linkedrecipe instead of mixing its steps into lasagna.
